hops.title: Where an elephant keeps its neurons
hops.text: An African elephant's brain weighs about three times as much as ours, so you might guess it packs far more neurons into its cerebral cortex. When Suzana Herculano-Houzel and colleagues counted the cells in one elephant's brain, it did hold 257 billion neurons, three times a human's total. But 97.5 percent of them, 251 billion, sat in the cerebellum. The elephant's cerebral cortex, twice the mass of ours, held only 5.6 billion neurons, about a third of the human count. Almost all of the extra neurons are cerebellar, which the authors suggest might be related to the elephant's sensorimotor specializations.

sources.citation: Herculano-Houzel et al., Front. Neuroanat. 8:46 (2014), PMID 24971054.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An African elephant carefully picking up a small acacia pod with the tip of its trunk.
image.caption: An African elephant keeps 97.5 percent of its 257 billion brain neurons in its cerebellum.

hops.title: A volunteer who wore reversing prisms for 27 days
hops.text: In a 1976 McGill University study, an adult volunteer wore head-mounted prisms that reversed left and right for 27 days. At first, the usual vestibulo-ocular reflex made the reversed image slip even farther across the retina with every sideways head turn. Within a week its gain had dropped to about a quarter of normal. By week three its timing had shifted 130 degrees and its gain had climbed back to half strength, close to running in reverse. It stayed that way even overnight. When the prisms came off on day 28, the timing recovered in two hours, but normal gain took another two to three weeks.

sources.citation: Gonshor & Melvill Jones, J. Physiol. 256(2):381–414 (1976), PMID 16992508.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Bulky vintage prism headgear resting on a wooden swivel chair in an old laboratory.
image.caption: After 27 days in left-right reversing prisms, a volunteer's eye reflex came close to running backwards.

hops.afterHeading: Predicting a lesion: what, which side, which region
hops.title: The roadside pen test and the cerebellum
hops.text: When a police officer holds a pen far to the side of a driver's face, one thing they watch for is the eye-holding problem doctors check for in cerebellar disease. Holding your gaze to the side depends on cerebellar circuits. When those circuits falter, the eyes drift back toward center and snap outward: gaze-evoked nystagmus. In a University Hospital Zurich study, 15 healthy volunteers drank enough alcohol to reach a blood alcohol level of 0.06 percent. Half an hour later, the speed of that inward drift had more than doubled, matching the pattern described in patients with late-onset cerebellar degeneration.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Close-up of eyes looking sideways to follow the tip of a silver pen.
image.caption: Alcohol weakens the cerebellum's hold on a sideways gaze, so the eyes drift back toward center.

audio.title: Three ways your cerebellum quietly runs the show
audio.transcript:
Most of the time, you never notice your cerebellum working, which is sort of the whole point. One of its jobs is to predict what your movements are about to do before your slow senses can report back. You notice that work most when the cerebellum is missing, tricked, or caught off guard.

Take a remarkable medical case published in two thousand fifteen by doctors in China. A twenty-four-year-old woman went to the hospital for dizziness, nausea, and a lifelong struggle to walk steadily. She was married, had a daughter, and understood and expressed herself well, though her speech was mildly slurred. Then came the C T and M R I scans. Doctors found no cerebellar tissue at all. The space at the back of her skull where it should have been was filled with fluid. She had been born without a cerebellum. Looking back at her history, the pieces fit. She stood on her own at age four, walked at seven, and her speech became understandable by six. She never learned to run or jump. On a neurological exam she had no weakness in any one part of her body, but she walked unsteadily and had mild to moderate trouble judging the distance when asked to touch her nose with her finger. A single case like this shows that a person can walk, talk, marry, and have a daughter without a cerebellum. What she could not do was move smoothly.

You can feel your own cerebellar predictions right now by trying to tickle the palm of your hand. Go ahead. It barely works, even though a friend making the exact same stroke would make you flinch. In nineteen ninety-eight and nineteen ninety-nine, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert, and Chris Frith tested why. Their brain scans pointed to the cerebellum: when you move, your cerebellum seems to predict the touch that will follow, giving your brain the signal it uses to turn down the incoming sensation. In a second experiment they built a clever setup with two small robots. Volunteers moved one robot arm with their left hand, which drove a second robot to stroke their right palm. When the robots stayed in sync, the touch felt dull. As the researchers added delay, up to about a fifth of a second, or made the hand move at a bigger angle to the stroke, volunteers rated it as more ticklish, as if the prediction no longer matched the touch.

Some learned predictions are so automatic that knowing better does not turn them off. Plenty of commuters know the odd stumble of stepping onto a broken escalator. You can stare right at the motionless steps, tell yourself they are not moving, and still lurch weirdly forward. In two thousand three, Raymond Reynolds and Adolfo Bronstein brought that stumble into a London lab with fourteen volunteers and a motorized sled moving at one point two meters per second. On their twenty walks onto the moving sled, volunteers walked faster than usual, at zero point nine meters per second instead of zero point six. Then the researchers stopped the sled and clearly warned everyone it would not move. Volunteers still stepped on too fast, at zero point seven one meters per second, pitched forward, and were surprised by their own legs. As Bronstein and colleagues later reported, even one or two rides can trigger that forward-sway after-effect, and deliberately trying to suppress it fails. Your conscious mind knows the steps are still, but the learned walking prediction, which Bronstein's team links to cortical and cerebellar structures, does not let go at once. In the lab, most measures were back to normal only by the second walk onto the still sled.
